Both corrections are applied after group normalization, which would otherwise cancel them, and both assume class-conditional noise. On wrong labels that follow the model’s own errors, the forward correction failed even when given the true noise rates [ 13 ] , and neither method has been tested against an exploitable false positive. VI-B Stronger Verifiers and Structural Checks The most common remedy is a better verifier, and offline accuracy buys less than one might expect. TinyV consults a 1.5B verifier only when the rule checker rejects, adding 2.6 to 2.8 points at 6 % extra step time, although its own false-positive rate is unreported [ 21 ] . xVerify, far more accurate than Math-Verify as a classifier, improves on it by only 0.8 points as a reward [ 36 ] , and a hybrid rule-then-model verifier adds 2.3 points for 25.7 % more training time [ 20 ] . Hardening targets exploitable false positives directly. Fine-tuning a judge with LoRA on discovered tokens cut mean false positives during GRPO from 655 to 42 over ten seeds (median 168 to 40) and prevented all eight false-positive collapses across two datasets, yet tokens found by a fresh discovery run still reach false-positive rates of 8.75 to 31 % against the hardened judges [ 25 ] . Training on truncated responses labeled incorrectly brings master-key false positives to 0.1 %, but has been tested only offline [ 8 ] . Structural checks close specific loopholes: an isomorphic verifier keeps the proxy–oracle gap near zero in inductive logic [ 23 ] , and consulting a PRM only when every rollout fails avoids the hacking seen when the PRM is the reward [ 37 ] . VI-C Data, Environments and Oracles Several errors are cheaper to remove at their source than to correct in the gradient. Re-verifying labels was the only remedy for wrong references [ 13 ] . A static audit of 16 samples per task predicts where leaky tests will reward wrong code, and repairing the 18 worst suites removes about half of that false-positive mass [ 22 ] . Filtering distillation data on true rather than proxy reward removes inherited hacking [ 31 ] . Hardening agentic graders cut exploits from 6.5 % to 0.8 % with task success unchanged [ 38 ] , and a Docker-gated loop repaired 9 of 11 hackable code tasks for $3.60 [ 7 ] . Access to a trusted oracle helps but does not cure: alternating with an oracle every 10 steps turns plateaus into delays; preventing collapse requires the oracle every 2 steps; and even then, the policy keeps producing the trigger [ 14 ] . VI-D Detecting and Suppressing Hacking Detection tells practitioners when hacking has begun, but does not stop it. Comparing ten trajectories raises an LLM detector’s macro-F1 from 0.45 to 0.63 on synthetic coding-agent hacks, but semantic hacks stay at 0.0 to 0.4 [ 39 ] . Probes on internal activations can flag hacking learned through fine-tuning [ 72 ] , and acting on the policy’s own representations goes further. A shortcut direction extracted from contrastive sentence pairs tracks hacking during training, and discounting the advantage of rollouts that score high on it cuts Phi-4-mini’s hack rate from 99.9 % to 24.9 % and lifts LeetCode pass@1 from 1.2 % to 12.0 %, whereas suppressing the same direction at generation time only lowers the hack rate to 72.3 % [ 30 ] . For correlated judges, confounder-aware aggregation beats majority voting on most benchmarks and neutralizes two master keys [ 40 ] , but in another study, aggregation closed at most 11 % of the gap to independent voting [ 28 ] , and neither has been tested inside RL. No mitigation has been shown to handle random, systematic, and exploitable errors simultaneously, and each defense against exploitable false positives rests on a single policy, judge, or task. Section VII asks how far these remedies carry when the reference itself is no longer trusted. VII Rewards Without a Trusted Reference (RQ4) When the reference comes from the policy, a rubric, or a judge, or when no checker is used, the earlier findings carry over with one change: the reward can no longer be checked against an independent source, so errors that such a check would expose become systematic by construction. VII-A Self-Generated Rewards When the group’s majority answer serves as the label [ 41 ] , label error and reward error come apart. At the start of training, only 37 % of majority labels were correct, yet 92 % of rewards were, because wrong answers rarely match a wrong majority [ 41 ] . The majority itself is wrong on 25.85 % of MATH-500 and 73.33 % of AIME 2024 questions in one study [ 46 ] . The regime decides the outcome. On small or test-time sets, such training helps, lifting Qwen2.5-Math-7B from 12.9 to 40.2 on AIME 2024 [ 41 ] . At the training-corpus scale, every intrinsic reward studied sharpens the initial distribution and eventually collapses, even in the most stable settings, by roughly 1,000 steps; in one majority-vote run, reward accuracy fell from about 0.80 to 0.48 within about 260 steps while the proxy reward kept rising [ 42 ] . Majority-vote baselines collapsed in several studies [ 73 , 74 , 47 ] , in one case with rollout accuracy falling from 44.0 % to 2.4 % while training reward rose [ 44 ] . Damage can also hide in aggregates. Pooled over three models, 21.6 % of problems were lost and only 0.7 % newly learned while pass@1 stayed flat or rose [ 43 ] , and about two-thirds of one audio gain came from a single phoneme template [ 75 ] . Coupling the reward to the online policy is no clear fix: a frozen self-certainty scorer was exploited near step 100 while the online one held for 150 steps [ 76 ] , but self-certainty collapsed in longer runs elsewhere [ 74 , 42 ] . Sparse external verification closes most of the gap. A Lean proof gate on the majority answer matched ground-truth reward on nine-benchmark averages for three models (e.g., 35.40 vs. 35.56) [ 45 ] , labels bought for 20 % of problems prevented collapse when targeted but not when random [ 47 ] , and soft vote weights from a tool verifier with only 25 to 39 % precision beat majority-vote training on all 15 model and benchmark pairs, whereas hard filtering on the same verifier hurt [ 46 ] . Stabilizers without any external signal delay collapse [ 74 , 73 , 44 , 77 , 78 ] but cannot correct a consensus that is systematically wrong [ 78 ] . VII-B Rubric and Judge Rewards Rubric judges, like answer judges, fail mostly by accepting. Against a panel of frontier models, a weak judge had 10.3 % false positives and 6.8 % false negatives on medical rubrics and 19.8 % and 4.4 % on science [ 9 ] , and on the harder half of disputed rubric items, balanced accuracy spans 55.65 % to 84.81 % across 18 judges [ 10 ] . The rubric adds an error of its own, since rubrics written without reference answers train worse policies (32.0 vs. 35.9 on HealthBench) [ 48 ] . In training, the share of newly credited criteria that were wrong grew from 39 % to 65 % under a weak medical judge. A strong judge showed no such trend, yet rubric-free judges still preferred the base model on 78.4 % of prompts, so a better verifier does not fix a misspecified rubric [ 9 ] . Exploitation again depends on discoverability. Injected judge biases were exploited after 68 to 478 steps, with less task-entangled biases exploited later, and two of the eight were never exploited [ 49 ] . Non-reasoning judges were hacked at every size, while reasoning judges moved the hacking to the gold judge, which the policy’s outputs also fooled, reaching an 89.6 % win rate on Arena-Hard-V2 creative writing [ 50 ] . Negated rubrics drive scores from 23.4 to 2.9, while incomplete ones degrade gracefully [ 79 ] , a split that, in our reading, mirrors J < 0 J<0 versus a smaller positive J J . Decomposing the reward and auditing training runs both help: a checklist judge is less accurate than specialized reward models on RewardBench yet trains better policies [ 80 ] , and a judge-blind auditing agent flagged all six hacked runs [ 49 ] . VII-C Verifier-Free Rewards Verifier-free methods drop the checker and reward the policy’s own probability of the reference answer. VeriFree does so after the policy’s reasoning, which equals exact-match RLVR in expectation when there is a single correct answer [ 51 ] . In our reading, it thereby trades the false positives of model verifiers for the false negatives of exact match, and adding equivalent answers helped only slightly [ 51 ] . RLPR rewards the mean token probability instead and reaches a ROC-AUC of about 0.90 against human labels on general data, against 0.61 for a rule verifier and 0.69 for a model verifier [ 52 ] . Probability rewards still under-credit correct paraphrases [ 53 ] , and the same method scores differently across papers that use different evaluation graders [ 52 , 53 ] , so the grader must be reported with the result. For the rubric and judge rewards, verifier error and specification error must be separated, because a better judge fixes only the first. Section VIII returns to this distinction. VIII Discussion The four research questions point to one conclusion: the harm a verifier error does is set less by its rate than by whether the policy can find and reproduce it, and the evidence for this is strong in a narrow set of settings and thin outside them. VIII-A Cross-Cutting Findings F1. Structure decides the regime; rate decides the cost within it. Exploitable false positives produce plateaus or collapse [ 14 , 8 , 25 , 26 , 23 ] , random errors mostly delay learning [ 17 , 11 , 12 ] , and systematic errors the policy cannot trigger degrade accuracy gradually or stay bounded [ 13 , 22 ] . Earlier RL theory points the same way, since a few corrupted states can cause near-worst-case regret [ 64 ] . Preference-based RL shows a similar pattern: feature-dependent noise significantly degrades a state-of-the-art noise-robust method in some settings, where a method without explicit denoising often does better [ 81 ] . The finding carries a qualifier, since under a fixed budget and a KL penalty, random errors also lower the endpoint, by an amount that depends strongly on the model [ 19 ] . F2. Error direction depends on what the checker checks and who built it. Answer-matching rules mostly reject [ 20 , 21 ] and generative judges mostly accept [ 18 , 61 ] , but rules that test a proxy property accept [ 23 ] , tests written by a model mostly reject [ 7 ] , and a reward model can be dominated by false negatives [ 19 ] . Because false positives cost more than false negatives at equal J J [ 17 ] , choosing rule rewards for their resistance to hacking [ 2 ] is sound, but a move from rules to judges trades a benign error for a dangerous one only when the judge’s false positives can be triggered. F3. Verifier error is non-stationary, and static accuracy is insufficient. Learned and self-generated verifiers lose accuracy as the policy changes [ 4 , 42 ] , and shortcut use rises with reasoning effort and longer RL [ 23 ] . For reference-based checkers, this is a hypothesis, backed mainly by a reference-free verifier outside RL [ 29 ] . Static accuracy predicts training direction only coarsely [ 32 ] : a PRM robust to gradient attacks was hacked in RL [ 26 ] , a far more accurate verifier added only 0.8 points as reward [ 36 ] , and a less accurate checklist judge trained better policies than specialized reward models [ 80 ] . F4. The evidence base is narrow and partly confounded. Of the 46 studies that train a policy, 44 use a Qwen model, trained policies rarely exceed 32B parameters, and most tasks are mathematical. Several central results rest on a single seed or a single policy and judge pair [ 19 , 9 , 25 , 49 ] , and contamination of Qwen2.5-Math on MATH-500 and AIME 2024 [ 34 ] threatens every result obtained with that model on those benchmarks. Training studies of agentic verification do not yet exist; the evidence there comes from audits [ 7 , 38 ] . F5. Self-generated rewards are bounded by the prior and rescued by sparse verification. Without an external check they sharpen and collapse at training-corpus scale [ 42 ] , though they can help on small or test-time sets [ 41 ] , and their damage can hide in aggregate metrics [ 43 , 75 ] . A small amount of external verification recovers most of the gap [ 45 , 47 , 46 ] . VIII-B Resolved and Open Disagreements Most apparent contradictions dissolve once the type of noise, the regime, or the budget is controlled. The claim that an imperfect verifier is good enough [ 11 , 12 ] and the finding that noisy data is destructive [ 13 ] concern different kinds of noise: random flips versus wrong labels that follow the model’s own errors. The apparent collapse at 50 % flips [ 12 ] is a failure to learn, as predicted at J = 0 J=0 [ 17 ] . Large losses under random noise [ 19 ] need not contradict the mean-field result, whose recovery of the clean endpoint holds without regularization [ 17 ] : that study used a fixed budget, a KL penalty and no ratio clipping, and under a KL penalty the dynamics settle at an interior equilibrium that depends on J J [ 17 ] , so longer training alone need not close the gap. Noise-aware corrections work on class-conditional noise [ 18 , 19 ] and fail on question-dependent labels [ 13 ] , and within-group correlation of rule failures [ 27 ] may reflect prompt difficulty rather than refute the independence those corrections assume. Four disagreements remain open. The mechanism behind spurious-reward gains is contested [ 33 , 34 , 35 ] . Online self-certainty was stable over short runs [ 76 ] but collapsed over longer ones [ 74 , 42 ] . Correlation-aware judge aggregation helped in one study [ 40 ] and closed a little of the gap in another [ 28 ] , and neither was tested in RL. Practitioners are advised both to prioritize precision [ 11 ] and to maximize J J rather than precision alone [ 17 ] , while a verifier with 25 to 39 % precision still helped as a soft vote weight [ 46 ] . VIII-C A Recommended Reporting Protocol Results are hard to compare because studies rarely report the verifier in enough detail to reproduce its errors. Table III lists recommended items, each motivated by a corpus result. The mean-field analysis of random errors [ 17 ] has no counterpart for response-dependent, exploitable errors under group-relative gradients, although corrupted-reward theory offers a starting point [ 64 ] , and, as noted in Section II , GRPO amplifies whatever the verifier accepts, false positives included. Empirically, verifier error should be measured on the policy’s own outputs as training proceeds [ 29 , 4 ] , the interaction between correlated errors and group size remains unexplored [ 27 , 28 ] , and defenses validated offline or on a single policy and judge pair need testing inside RL [ 8 , 40 , 25 ] . Three further problems follow from the corpus: separating verifier error from rubric misspecification [ 9 , 48 ] , guarding against hacking of the oracle itself [ 50 ] , and preventing hacking inherited through distillation data [ 31 ] . Agentic and long-horizon verification has been audited [ 7 , 38 ] but not yet studied in training. VIII-E Limitations Our synthesis has two limitations. First, studies differ in models, budgets, and reference standards, so we compare directions and regimes, not effect sizes. Second, the search, based on keywords and four seed studies [ 14 , 11 , 6 , 27 ] , covered English-language work up to September 2026 and may miss work framed in other terms. IX Conclusion and Future Work This work surveyed 58 studies of verifier errors in RLVR. The evidence shows that the harm an error causes depends less on its rate than on whether the policy can find and reproduce it: exploitable false positives cause plateaus or collapse, random errors mostly slow learning, and errors that the policy cannot trigger degrade accuracy gradually or stay bounded. Whether a verifier errs by rejecting or accepting depends on what it checks and who built it, and its errors shift as the policy improves, so accuracy measured before training says little about robustness during it. Most mitigations have been tested against a single kind of error, and self-generated rewards remain bounded by the model’s prior unless some external verification is added. We therefore argue for treating the verifier as a component to be measured on the policy’s own outputs, probed adversarially, and reported in full. Open directions include a theory of exploitable errors, defenses validated inside RL across several policies and judges, and training studies of agentic verification.
